  "title": "Wrong First Impression",
  "description": "Expanded Series Bible III #10 Wrong First Impression reusable adult idea source: the engine generates substantial but believable mistaken first impressions between adult {{char}} and {{user}} — misread identities, misleading circumstances, reputation errors and incompatible assumptions — then varies who was wrong, why the mistake was reasonable, how quickly evidence contradicts it and how the correction lands.",
  "source_version": "1.0",
  "bible": {
    "document": "Character Card Forge — Series Bible III",
    "version": "0.4",
    "entry": "10",
    "kind": "series"
  },
  "summary": "The opening centres on a substantial but believable mistaken impression between adults. {{char}} may initially misread {{user}} — taking him for a colleague, a client, a stranger, an intruder, a rival, a date or something he is not — or {{user}} may be handed circumstances that make {{char}} look very different from reality: an inherited nickname, a mis-sent message, borrowed clothes, a case of mistaken identity, an old reputation or misleading timing. Both may begin with incompatible assumptions and only gradually discover the mismatch. The mistake should be reasonable given the available evidence, the correction can be embarrassing, funny, irritating or genuinely consequential, and every outcome — friendship, rivalry, romance, partnership or nothing — stays open.",
  "core_premise": "Two adults meet while at least one holds a significant but plausible false impression about the other, formed through ordinary inference errors, incomplete context, misleading timing, secondhand reputation, mistaken identity or deliberate encouragement by a third party. This is not automatically a secret-identity story. The engine is the gap between what the characters reasonably believe and what is actually true: how they act on the wrong assumption, how and when contradicting evidence appears, and what the correction costs or earns. {{char}}'s mistaken assumptions about {{user}} are her beliefs, never objective truth, and {{user}}'s reaction to being misjudged — amusement, offence, correction, exploitation of the misunderstanding or silence — remains entirely his choice.",
  "setup": "Create a non-graphic adult roleplay opening built on a mistaken first impression. Specify who holds the false impression and what it is, why it was reasonable to form given the available evidence, the setting and circumstance that produced it, whether anyone deliberately encouraged the misunderstanding, and how close the first contradicting clue sits to the surface. Establish {{char}} as a complete adult person — occupation, interests, temperament, her own possible blind spots — acting on her wrong assumption at a playable moment: a greeting aimed at the wrong identity, a frosty reception, an over-familiar welcome, an accusation, a proposition or an apology offered to the wrong man. Do not write {{user}}'s feelings, dialogue, corrections or decisions, and do not predetermine whether the misunderstanding resolves warmly, badly, hilariously or not at all.",
  "core_variables": [
    "Who holds the mistaken impression: {{char}} about {{user}}, {{user}} about {{char}}, or both about each other in incompatible ways.",
    "What caused the mistake: mistaken identity, incomplete context, secondhand reputation, misleading timing, an honest misread of behaviour or appearance, or deliberate encouragement by someone else.",
    "How reasonable the mistake was: nearly unavoidable given the evidence, plausible but hasty, or a lazy stereotype the character chose not to verify.",
    "How quickly evidence contradicting the impression appears: within the first conversation, within days, or only after the relationship has developed.",
    "Whether anyone intentionally encouraged the misunderstanding, and why — protection, mischief, jealousy, convenience or agenda.",
    "Whether the correction is embarrassing, funny, irritating, professionally consequential, personally devastating or quietly relieving.",
    "How {{char}} reacts to being wrong: apology, doubling down, laughter, withdrawal, curiosity, guilt or defensiveness.",
    "What {{char}}'s mistaken assumption actually is about {{user}}: his job, wealth, availability, sexuality, intentions, past, danger or personality.",
    "How {{user}} is situationally framed at the meeting: replacement colleague, blind date, new tenant, security escort, delivery, relative of someone, or the wrong name entirely.",
    "Whether the two share prior history neither has recognised, and whether the impression hides or distorts it.",
    "What stakes ride on the first impression: a job, a friendship group, a landlord relationship, a team, a family introduction or a reputation.",
    "Whether {{char}} treats her assumption as established fact or entertains doubts she suppresses.",
    "How much of the mistake {{char}} owns up to voluntarily versus is confronted with.",
    "Whether resolving the misunderstanding is even wanted, or whether living with the false impression suits one of them.",
    "What the corrected picture reveals about {{char}}: her generosity with wrong guesses, her snobbery, her nosiness, her fairness or her jumpiness.",
    "Whether the episode becomes a shared joke, a lasting grudge, a foundation story or a caution between them.",
    "Where the opening lands: before the reveal, mid-reveal, or after the correction with its consequences still unfolding.",
    "How much the misunderstanding permanently changes the trajectory versus being a bump the players can route around."
  ],
  "generation_rules": [
    "Do not write {{user}} for the player or define {{user}}'s feelings, decisions, dialogue, consent, intentions, future behaviour, or whether he corrects, exploits or ignores the misunderstanding unless the source explicitly supplies that fact.",
    "Character belief is not objective truth: {{char}}'s mistaken impression of {{user}} remains her belief, however reasonable, and must never be narrated as established fact about him.",
    "Do not pre-play outcomes. Whether the reveal lands as comedy, embarrassment, offence, apology, romance, rivalry, friendship or nothing remains roleplay space.",
    "All romantic or sexual characters are adults.",
    "This is not automatically a secret-identity story. Prefer ordinary human inference errors, incomplete context, misleading timing, case of mistaken identity, or reputation rather than hidden double lives unless a generated variant explicitly chooses one.",
    "The mistaken impression must be reasonable given the available evidence. A character who jumps to conclusions should have a plausible reason for the leap.",
    "Do not force romance, sex, friendship or reconciliation out of the correction. Amusement, wariness, professional courtesy, distance or a clean reset are all valid.",
    "Sex or attraction, if it appears, must not erase personality: the correction can sting, flatter, bore or unsettle independently of romance.",
    "Do not make the misunderstood {{user}} secretly superior — wealth, status or hidden talent is optional, never the default payoff of being misjudged.",
    "Do not make the misunderstanding automatically flattering to {{char}} either: she may look prejudiced, nosy, careless or foolish once corrected, and that is a legitimate outcome.",
    "If a third party engineered the misunderstanding, give them a coherent motive; their interference does not strip the leads of responsibility for their own assumptions.",
    "Keep correction and consequence separate: the reveal itself should not bundle a mandatory reward, punishment, apology or confession.",
    "Characters should remain people outside the hook: occupation, hobbies, friends, values and non-mistake-related personality persist before, during and after the reveal.",
    "Vary the size of the mistake: a trivial wrong-name comedy and a life-altering professional misidentification are both in range.",
    "Do not require the misunderstanding to be resolved within the opening; some of the best versions sustain it well into play or leave it standing.",
    "The first contradicting evidence should exist somewhere in reach; a mistake with no possible discovery collapses into pure farce or pure suspense — choose deliberately.",
    "Consent is activity-specific: an apology, a laugh or shared amusement over the mix-up does not imply touch, dating or intimacy.",
    "British/Australian spellings; keep all content non-graphic and foreground the human comedy, tension or drama of mistaken belief rather than explicit material.",
    "Do not script other bystanders' reactions as unanimous: colleagues, friends or family may find the mix-up funnier, crueler or less important than the leads do.",
    "Overlap boundary: distinct from You're Not Who I Expected, which builds on true prior history whose details have changed; here at least one party's belief is factually wrong at the start. Cross-link when both apply.",
    "Overlap boundary: distinct from Her Hidden Side, where the truth is concealed by the character herself; here the false belief can arise with no deception from the misjudged party at all.",
    "Overlap boundary: distinct from What Are You Doing Here?, where surprise comes from unexpected place-based recognition; here the surprise is about who the other person is, not where they are.",
    "Generate the impression, the evidence and the correction timing independently — a slow reveal with a silly mistake can outperform a fast reveal with a serious one.",
    "Do not predetermine whether {{user}} ever corrects the impression, confirms it for his own convenience, or lets {{char}} discover it by accident; all three are valid player strategies.",
    "Open at a playable moment where the mistaken impression is actively shaping behaviour: the reveal, its build-up or its immediate aftermath."
  ],
  "guardrails": [
    "All participants are adults; every interaction is non-graphic and consent-forward.",
    "{{char}}'s mistaken beliefs about {{user}} are her assumptions, never narrator-endorsed facts.",
    "No scripting of {{user}}'s feelings, corrections, dialogue, consent or future behaviour.",
    "Do not pre-play outcomes: apology, laughter, offence, romance, friendship, rivalry or indifference all remain open.",
    "The mistaken impression must be believable given available evidence; no absurd contrivance disguised as human error.",
    "Being misjudged does not make {{user}} secretly better or worse than the impression; hidden superiority is optional, never default.",
    "Being wrong does not reduce {{char}} to a fool; her reaction should match her established personality.",
    "Third-party manipulation, if present, has a coherent motive and does not dissolve the leads' own responsibility.",
    "Consent is activity-specific: shared amusement, apology or gratitude does not imply touch, dating or sex.",
    "No forced romance from the correction; professional, platonic, cool or adversarial continuations are equally valid.",
    "No humiliation kink, punishment or revenge as a mandatory consequence of the misunderstanding.",
    "Preserve each character's life beyond the hook: job, interests, friends and boundaries survive the reveal.",
    "If the impression touches on reputation (criminal, romantic, professional), keep rumours distinct from verified facts in the narration."
  ],
  "diversity_axes": [
    "Who is wrong: {{char}} about {{user}}, {{user}} about {{char}}, both mutually, or a whole group wrong about one person.",
    "Cause of the impression: mistaken identity, partial information, secondhand gossip, misleading appearance, borrowed belongings, an overheard fragment, or a deliberate set-up.",
    "Reasonableness: virtually unavoidable, plausible but unverified, or a prejudiced shortcut the character privately knows is unfair.",
    "Speed of contradiction: during the first exchange, within the first week, or only after the relationship has deepened.",
    "Content of the false belief: wrong job, wrong wealth level, wrong availability, wrong intentions, wrong danger level, wrong personality, wrong name or wrong history.",
    "Emotional tone of the correction: mortifying, hilarious, irritating, chilling, professionally serious, quietly relieving or bittersweet.",
    "{{char}}'s handling of being wrong: graceful apology, deflecting humour, stubborn doubling-down, mortified retreat, eager over-correction or defensive counter-accusation.",
    "Third parties: no one involved, a meddling matchmaker, a jealous rival, a protective friend, a bored colleague or a family member with an agenda.",
    "Setting: workplace, apartment block, university-of-adults, small town, event, wedding, hospital, shop, club, holiday, online-to-offline handoff.",
    "Stakes of the first impression: none beyond social awkwardness, a job or contract, a tenancy, a friendship group's opinion, a family's approval, a team position.",
    "Prior history: strangers, acquaintances who misremember, people connected through a third party, or two people hiding a shared past.",
    "Whether anyone benefits from the misunderstanding and quietly resists correcting it.",
    "Relationship outcome: friends, colleagues, rivals, partners, lovers, distant acquaintances or people who agree to forget it.",
    "Whether the story opens pre-reveal, mid-reveal or post-correction.",
    "Scale: a single wrong sentence and a life-defining misidentification sit at opposite ends of the same axis."
  ],
  "cross_links": [
    "You're Not Who I Expected — sibling series built on true prior history where the other person has genuinely changed; here the belief is factually wrong from the start, and the two can chain when the mistaken impression is corrected into an unexpected reunion.",
    "Her Hidden Side — the truth is concealed by the character herself there; here the misjudged party may have deceived no one, though a variant can combine both.",
    "What Are You Doing Here? — surprise of place versus surprise of identity; a corrected first impression at an impossible location naturally crosses into it.",
    "We Used to Know Each Other — mutual misidentification of someone half-remembered can route into this reconnection series once identities resolve.",
    "We Matched — profiles and messages create deliberate self-presentation, so an inaccurate first impression at the real-world meeting belongs here.",
    "The Other Regular — a habitué mistaken for staff, owner or a fellow regular of a different kind fits the recurring-venue engine.",
    "Set Up Together — a third-party set-up is a natural engine for engineered wrong impressions; cross when the matchmaker's framing was false.",
    "Convention Meetup — online handles meeting offline invite both mistaken-identity and expectation-mismatch versions."

  "raw_prompt": "Generate a non-graphic adult character-card premise for Wrong First Impression. At least one adult holds a substantial but believable false first impression about the other: a mistaken identity, wrong job or wealth, misread intentions, a misleading reputation or a third party's deliberate embellishment. Vary who is wrong and who is wronged, how reasonable the inference was, how quickly contradicting evidence appears, what the correction costs or earns, and whether anyone engineered the error. Character belief is never objective truth and the narration must keep assumptions distinct from facts. Do not script {{user}}'s feelings, corrections or decisions; whether the reveal lands as comedy, offence, apology or nothing is open, and friendship, rivalry, romance, partnership or a clean reset are all valid outcomes. Open where the mistaken impression is actively shaping behaviour. All participants are adults; consent, boundaries and player agency are non-negotiable."
